Jusqu’à récemment, Montréal était connue: Until recently, Montréal was known as a city with affordable rents, even for broke artists. But in recent years, the metropolis, like other major cities across Canada, has been shaken by a housing crisis.
Le 24 avril dernier, des centaines de lo: On April 24, hundreds of tenants and housing groups from across the province marched through the Plateau-Mont-Royal. Their demands? A rent freeze, a provincial rent registry and a moratorium on evictions. They want to start a real dialogue with the Minister of Housing and are calling on the City to be stricter with its own regulations.
À cette occasion, Cédric Dussault, porte: On that occasion, Cédric Dussault, spokesperson for the Regroupement des comités logement et associations de locataires du Québec (RCLALQ), addressed the crowd behind the Mont-Royal metro station.
« La libre négociation entre propriétair: “Free negotiation between landlords and tenants in the current context simply doesn’t exist,” he said. “Not in a context of exploding rents (...) where a large number of tenants live under the constant threat of a fraudulent eviction or a bad-faith repossession of their unit.”
Plusieurs protestataires brandissaient d: Several protesters held signs calling for the resignation of Minister of Housing France-Élaine Duranceau, who was previously a real estate broker. Representatives of housing committees say she has never spoken with them, but often meets with landlords.
<l1>À Montréal, en 2023</l1>, le loyer m: <l1>In Montréal in 2023</l1>, the average advertised rent for a 3½ was $1,805, an increase of nearly 14% in one year. On top of that, Montréal’s <l2>vacancy rate</l2> was 1.5% at the time.
« C’est une crise multiple qui engendre: “It’s a multi-layered crisis that is creating a public health crisis,” says Annie Lapalme, community organizer at Entraide Logement Hochelaga-Maisonneuve.
« Nous, on pense que c’est même une cris: “We think it’s even a humanitarian crisis. It affects every aspect of people’s lives. The people who go to food banks do so because they can no longer pay for their housing, which has become too expensive. We can’t go on like this, we’re heading straight for a wall,” she says angrily.
Autre point d’achoppement, selon elle :: Another sticking point, she says: short-term rentals. “The City regularly says it will take action against Airbnb. Right now, we have tons of them in [Hochelaga-Maisonneuve], but the borough passes the buck to Quebec City. Quebec City doesn’t do much, so it’s constantly someone else’s problem,” she says.
Claude Jalette (première de la gauche) d: Claude Jalette (first from left) says building new housing isn’t enough to fight crushing rents in Trois-Rivières. Photo: Emelia Fournier
Claude Jalette est venue de Trois-Rivièr: Claude Jalette came from Trois-Rivières to take part in the march. Accompanied by five other people, she carried a sign that read: “Housing crisis – Legault is slow!” The Infologis coordinator told us that building new housing isn’t enough: five years after construction, landlords can raise their rent each year by whatever amount they see fit.
« La classe moyenne aussi se fait complè: “The middle class is also being completely impoverished by new buildings [less than] five years old, where there is no standard [for an acceptable rent increase],” she says.
Roxanne Deniger, du Centre d’éducation e: Roxanne Deniger, of the Centre d’éducation et d’action des femmes (CEAF) de Montréal, points out that access to affordable housing is essential to women’s safety.
« [Plusieurs d’entre elles] ne quittent: “[Many of them] don’t leave their homes because of domestic violence. We’re also thinking of women with children who are struggling to find housing in an increasingly difficult economic context,” she says.

Les difficultés de logement, Julien* et: Julien* and Patricia Garcia know something about housing struggles. Neighbours for seven years on the Plateau-Mont-Royal, the two friends teamed up in a legal fight against their landlord.
Malgré sa petite taille, Patricia, qui a: Despite her small size, Patricia, who is 71, takes up a lot of space with her sweeping gestures. Her face is expressive. She is both smiling and serious as she talks about her love for her Plateau community and the damage caused by gentrification.
Julien est chaleureux et doux avec Patri: Julien is warm and gentle with Patricia, but when he talks about his problems with his landlord, he transforms, so to speak, into a lawyer: informed, passionate and in search of justice.
Les deux payent chacun environ 1 000 $ p: Each of them pays about $1,000 a month for a multi-bedroom apartment, a rarity on the Plateau. Patricia lives in a renovated former garage, where she runs her aesthetics business. That’s where we meet.
Selon eux, leur propriétaire cherche à l: According to them, their landlord is trying to evict them from their building, which could push them out of the neighbourhood. “It’s terrible. I’m looking for apartments close to here. There aren’t any. And if you move a studio from its spot, you lose clients!” Patricia laments.
Elle vit sur le Plateau depuis qu’elle a: She has lived on the Plateau since she immigrated from Mexico 35 years ago. In this neighbourhood, she can do everything on foot: run her errands, visit her two daughters and her granddaughter, and go to the parks. “I couldn’t change neighbourhoods. It’s impossible. I’ll do everything I can to stay here, to be next to my daughters,” she says.
Les deux locataires, à tour de rôle, nou: The two tenants, taking turns, told us about the stress and hardship they have lived through for several years with their new landlord.
Depuis qu’une société a pris possession: Since a company took possession of their building in 2021, the four other units in the building have been converted into <l1>Airbnb apartments, with rents of more than $4,000 a month</l1>.
Le nouveau propriétaire a envoyé un avis: The new landlord sent an eviction notice as soon as he took possession of the building: “We intend to repossess your unit at the end of your fixed-term lease in order to subdivide your unit.”
Julien a consulté un avocat. Des règleme: Julien consulted a lawyer. City bylaws that came into force in 2022 prohibit the subdivision of residential units. Once informed, the new landlord withdrew his eviction notice. But little by little, he managed to convince the other tenants to leave their homes.
« Avec la COVID, quand tout le monde dev: “During COVID, when everyone had to stay home, we had coffee outside. [Among neighbours], we were all friends. Now it’s really terrible living with Airbnbs in the building. I don’t feel safe in my apartment. There are strangers everywhere. Sometimes they think my apartment is an Airbnb. They try to open the door, they look through the windows, they take my things. Outside, they make a lot of noise; they’re disrespectful because there’s no established relationship,” he says.
Patricia assure que la hausse continuell: Patricia says the continual rise in rents and the presence of Airbnbs “are degrading the quality of life of Montrealers” in the middle class. “The worst part of all this is that people are being put out on the street and uprooted from their neighbourhood, all because of the desire to make a lot of money,” she says indignantly.
Patricia Garcia lutte pour garder son lo: Patricia Garcia is fighting to keep her affordable housing in the Plateau-Mont-Royal. Photo: Emelia Fournier
Dans une lettre envoyée en juin 2022, le: In a letter sent in June 2022, their landlord asked them to leave the building in October for a period of eight months in order to “completely redo all the units in the property and bring them up to date.”
Craignant que cette évacuation soit plus: Fearing that this evacuation would be more than temporary and that the landlord would impose a rent increase after his renovations, Patricia and Julien then found themselves in a race against the work.
Leur avocat, Daniel Crespo, estime que l: Their lawyer, Daniel Crespo, believes that landlords often take advantage of temporary evacuations to carry out renovictions.
« Le problème, c’est qu’il y a beaucoup: “The problem is that there are many inconveniences resulting from this temporary evacuation, so it often turns into a permanent one. If the landlord fails to negotiate a permanent evacuation, he takes advantage of the tenant’s supposedly temporary absence to do the renovation and immediately rent to someone else. In doing so, he prevents the original tenant from returning to the apartment,” he explains.
Pendant deux ans, Patricia et Julien ont: For two years, Patricia and Julien had to bear legal costs, attend pre-hearings and adapt to changes in hearing dates. Finally, a hearing was set by the <l1>Administrative Housing Tribunal (TAL)</l1> for April 2024.
Patricia a vécu beaucoup de stress en ra: Patricia went through a lot of stress because of all this uncertainty. “I had a bit of a depression, I had trouble sleeping with all this terrible stress of facing a man who wants more money,” she says.
Mais le jour précédant l’audience, son p: But the day before the hearing, her landlord dropped the case. Daniel Crespo assumes the landlord couldn’t show that the major renovations were essential.
« Bien sûr, on était contents de ne pas: “Of course, we were happy not to go before the TAL, not to have to wait for a ruling to see whether we would win or not,” Julien sums up. “At the same time, we had already prepared all our documents. We had already paid a lot for lawyers. So [the damage] was already done, even though he dropped it at the last minute like that.”
Julien a cinq autres dossiers en cours a: Julien has five other cases pending at the TAL with his landlord. “A kind of legal guerrilla warfare” is how Daniel Crespo describes the landlord’s manoeuvres against his client.
Dans un des dossiers, il est ainsi allég: In one of the cases, it is alleged that Julien did not cooperate in the installation of Internet cables for the Airbnbs.
« C’est une demande frivole, qui n’a pas: “It’s a frivolous claim with no factual basis. The claim is for $1,500. It has already taken up three hours of hearing, and we’re not done. All of this is far more than $1,500 in legal fees… The goal here isn’t for the landlord to recover the amount he believes Julien cost him, it’s really just to wear him down,” Daniel Crespo says.
Le TAL ne peut cependant pas refuser de: However, the TAL cannot refuse to hear cases submitted by landlords, no matter how often they file.
« Il y a cette espèce d’asymétrie qui pe: “There’s this kind of asymmetry that allows landlords to spend, spend, spend on legal fees, but it also reveals their intent,” says Daniel Crespo.
Il existe un moyen pour que les locatair: There is one way for tenants to learn about their rights: housing committees, which provide them with advice and information.
Marie-Ève d’Entremont, organisatrice com: Marie-Ève d’Entremont, community organizer at the <l1>Comité logement du Plateau Mont-Royal</l1> (CLPMR), is getting more and more calls from tenants who want to fight major rent increases. On the Plateau, in 2021, <l2>32%</l2> of households spent more than 30% of their income on housing.
<l1>Au cours des quatre</l1> dernières a: <l1>Over the past four</l1> years, the number of consultations at the CLPMR has risen by 81%. “And it’s not just us, it’s all the housing committees!” says Marie-Ève d’Entremont.
Cette progression de la demande est auss: This rise in demand is also due to the underfunding of the <l1>Administrative Housing Tribunal (TAL)</l1>, which is run by the provincial government, she explains.
« Les employés sont brûlés. Ils ne sont: “The employees are burned out. They aren’t able to answer the phone [to give advice]. It’s super hard for tenants to talk to someone because the employees are simply at their limit. Answering this kind of question is part of the Administrative Housing Tribunal’s mandate,” she says.
Elle encourage tous les locataires à com: She encourages all tenants to contact their housing committee for advice. Tenants always have the right to refuse a rent increase or a no-cause eviction notice, she reminds us. “On your own, you can feel completely overwhelmed. But when you meet other tenants and get organized, you take back power on the ground,” she concludes.
Cédric Dussault, porte-parole du RCLALQ,: Cédric Dussault, spokesperson for RCLALQ, believes that fighting the housing crisis requires going beyond simply knowing your rights.
Il dit que la Ville n’est pas assez stri: He says the City isn’t strict enough with landlords, particularly when it comes to the spread of Airbnbs and building maintenance. “The City even has the power to expropriate offending landlords. There are a lot of steps before getting there, but ultimately, the City could do it. Obviously, it’s a power it never uses,” he says.
Selon lui, les trois paliers de gouverne: In his view, all three levels of government misunderstand the crisis by blaming it on a lack of housing. “This idea that the fundamental problem of the housing crisis is a question of supply, it’s false. It’s magical thinking,” he says.
Il montre du doigt la concentration de l: He points to the concentration of real estate ownership. A <l1>study published in 2023</l1> indicates that less than 1% of landlords in the metropolis own nearly 32% of Montréal’s rental stock.
« Les grandes sociétés immobilières ont: “Big real estate companies can afford to pay more [for buildings]. So, as they drive up prices, buildings become less and less accessible to smaller landlords. That allows the big real estate companies to buy even more. It’s a phenomenon that is accelerating. We don’t have a monopoly, but a concentration that means the market is controlled by a minority of landlords.”
Cédric Dussault, porte-parole du RCLALQ,: Cédric Dussault, spokesperson for RCLALQ, addresses protesters during Tenants’ Day. Photo: Regroupement des comités-logement et associations de locataires
Martin Messier, le président de l’Associ: Martin Messier, president of the Association des Propriétaires du Québec (APQ), also believes that small landlords are in a very precarious situation right now, notably because of higher interest rates and rising insurance costs.
« On n’est pas plus capables. Quand il f: “We’re no better off. When I have to get a roof redone, it costs me three times what it used to, and my insurance costs me five times more. Everything is going up,” he explains.
Il estime que tous les règlements et l’e: He believes that all the regulations and the overall costs in Quebec mean less investment in housing construction, but adds a bit later that this isn’t necessarily a disadvantage for landlords: “We’re not building many units. Since there’s no housing, we can charge what it costs us and make money on top of that. There isn’t much competition. It’s a factor in rising prices,” says Mr. Messier.
Au lieu d’aller perdre une journée au TA: Instead of losing a day at the TAL, Martin Messier thinks landlords should provide a detailed justification of their costs and clearly explain rent increases to their tenants.
« Je pense que ça prend une meilleure co: “I think it takes better communication. Often, people refuse [the increase] because it’s too expensive. But the tenant should take the time to ask why their rent is going up. And to landlords, [I say] the same thing: you have to tell [the tenant], ‘Look, I’ll explain it to you, the calculation grid I filled out with the TAL.’”
Marie Sterlin, conseillère d’arrondissem: Marie Sterlin, borough councillor in the Plateau-Mont-Royal, is supporting Julien in his case. She pushed through a new regulation that prohibits converting a residential unit into an Airbnb apartment in the neighbourhood.
Mais elle dit faire face à une résistanc: But she says she is facing resistance from landlords. “We have an opposition that is really getting organized. But we haven’t given up,” she says.
La ville a reçu un signalement des Airbn: The City received a report about the Airbnbs in Julien and Patricia’s building. This type of apartment is not permitted unless it is the owner’s primary residence. However, the report led nowhere.
« Une fois qu’une plainte est déposée, c: “Once a complaint is filed, it’s very hard to prove that someone is running an Airbnb. It’s only with the province’s help that we’ll succeed; they have the resources. The province can check tax returns and ask, ‘How come you have two addresses?’” explains M<sup>s</sup>. Sterlin.
Elle considère en outre que les amendes: She also believes that fines aren’t enough to deter some landlords. She regrets that the City is not currently exploring the possibility of expropriating the buildings of offending landlords, as suggested by RCLALQ.
Le 22 mai, la ministre Duranceau a propo: On May 22, Minister Duranceau proposed a <l1>three-year moratorium on </l1>evictions “to subdivide the unit, substantially enlarge it or change its use.” But even if this bill is passed, for Julien and Patricia, the fight is far from over.
Ils doivent retourner devant le TAL pour: They have to go back before the TAL to contest major rent increases and fear new manoeuvres from their landlord. But Julien and Patricia say that together, they will keep fighting for their rights.
« Il y a quelque chose là-dedans qui ne: “There’s something in all this that isn’t working, and we’re going to solve it together. You can’t evict tenants just because someone wants to make thousands of extra dollars. We’re not going to give up,” Patricia adds.
Le propriétaire de Julien et de Patricia: Julien and Patricia’s landlord declined to speak with La Converse. As for the Minister of Housing, she did not respond to our interview request.
